entries.clue: Repeatedly stretch point? (4,5,4)

blocks.note: a stretch is a spell in prison, which is time served
a point is a moment of time — 'at that point' is 'at that time' — and the answer names in full the relation of one coming after the other

annotation.surface: Bending a rule further than you should, over and over.
annotation.walkthrough: Nothing in the clue says 'after': the phrase supplies it, and the question mark is the setter owning up. Stretch and point are both time, one of them long and one of them instant.
annotation.definitionFit: Doing something time after time is doing it repeatedly; the phrase is the idiom for endless recurrence.

entries.clue: When empty, rule 1 is to fill glasses for salutations (8)

indicatorNotes.When empty: a word emptied has had its insides taken out, leaving the letters at either end
indicatorNotes.to fill: filling something means going inside it, so this letter is dropped into the middle

blocks.note: RULE with its middle emptied keeps R…E
specs are glasses
the answer at 1 down is TIME, and t is the abbreviation for it

annotation.surface: The first rule of hosting: keep everyone's glass topped up for the toasts.
annotation.walkthrough: It is 'rule' that gets emptied, not 'when' — the comma is placed to make you try the wrong word. The number is a cross-reference to 1 down, which supplies a single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: To pay your respects is to send salutations; both words are the plural noun for a formal greeting.

entries.clue: Group left in trouble in retirement (4)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts the piece before it inside the piece after it
indicatorNotes.in retirement: something in retirement has gone back, and letters going back are written in reverse

blocks.note: the rub is the trouble — 'there's the rub'
l = left

annotation.surface: Someone abandoned in difficulty the moment their working life ends.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Group' is pointing at Britpop rather than at any collection of things — the band took their name from a verb meaning to smudge. Two 'in's do different jobs, one enclosing and one turning round.
annotation.definitionFit: Blur are a British band, and a band is a group — definition by example, with the capital hidden by the clue's first word.

entries.clue: News account breaking down summit (8)

indicatorNotes.breaking: breaking into something means getting inside it, so these letters go in the middle

blocks.note: pile is the soft raised surface of a carpet or velvet, as down is the soft covering on a bird
n = new, and the s makes it plural: two of them
a/c = account

annotation.surface: A news report of a summit meeting collapsing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'News' is the trick: not information at all, but N for new made plural. The summit is a mountain top, not the conference the surface has convened.
annotation.definitionFit: A pinnacle is the topmost point of anything — the summit of a mountain, or of a career.

entries.clue: Folly of international firm returning self-assembly boxes (6)

indicatorNotes.returning: something returning comes back the way it went, so its letters are written backwards
indicatorNotes.boxes: to box something is to shut it in a box, so these letters close around it

blocks.note: i = international
DIY — do it yourself — is what self-assembly furniture asks of you
a firm is a CO, turned back to front

annotation.surface: An international company foolishly shipping its flat-pack cartons back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boxes' is the verb, to enclose — not the cartons the surface is loading onto a lorry. The firm turns round and lands inside DIY, with the international letter already waiting at the front.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiocy is behaviour without sense, which is what folly names.

entries.clue: Thrash a legal case for trial out – it’s iron-clad (10)

indicatorNotes.out: letters that are out are out of their proper order, so they need rearranging
indicatorNotes.case: the case of a word is the shell it comes in — its outermost letters
indicatorNotes.clad: to be clad is to be covered, so these two letters wrap round the outside

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
the case of TriaL is T…L
anagram indicator
iron is Fe on the periodic table, and it clads the rest: F in front, E behind

annotation.surface: Demolishing the case someone has brought to court, with an argument nothing can dent.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Iron-clad' does two jobs at once: the chemical symbol, and the instruction to wrap it round everything else. Taking the 'case' of a word — its outer letters — is a device worth filing away.
annotation.definitionFit: To flagellate is to whip, and a thrashing is a whipping; both are the plain verb for beating.

entries.clue: If not, French articles succeeded (6)

blocks.note: un is the French for 'a'
les is the French 'the' in front of a plural
s = succeeded

annotation.surface: Otherwise, it was the pieces written in French that did well.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Articles' is plural for a reason: the wordplay wants two of them, and French keeps a whole drawerful. The grammar-book words are worth collecting — UN, UNE, LE, LA, LES.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Unless it rains' and 'if it does not rain' set the same condition, so the two open a clause the same way.

entries.clue: Model bounced online to experience ecstasy (2,2,5,4)

indicatorNotes.Model: to model something is to mould it, and letters moulded afresh come out in another order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, thirteen letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A model thrown off the internet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Model' looks like the noun the surface needs and is really a verb: to model is to shape. Ecstasy here is the feeling rather than the pill, which is why the answer is a state of mind.
annotation.definitionFit: To be on cloud nine is to be blissfully happy — the idiom for experiencing ecstasy.

entries.clue: Regularly birdie and occasionally eagle – perfect (5)

indicatorNotes.Regularly: something done regularly happens at a fixed interval, so the letters are taken at a fixed interval too
indicatorNotes.occasionally: occasionally means now and then rather than throughout, so only some of the letters are used

blocks.note: every second letter of b-I-r-D-i-E
every second letter of e-A-g-L-e

annotation.surface: A golfer's card: birdies most rounds, an eagle now and again.
annotation.walkthrough: Two extractions of the same kind, from a pair of words that sit together naturally: in golf a birdie is one under par and an eagle two. Both runs start at the second letter.
annotation.definitionFit: An ideal arrangement is a perfect one; the adjective slots in wherever 'perfect' would.

entries.clue: Laziness in Céline Dion cast – one is dropped (9)

indicatorNotes.cast: cast means thrown, and letters thrown down land in a new order
indicatorNotes.is dropped: what is dropped is left out of the letters you build with

blocks.note: the singer's name less one I: nine letters to rearrange
one = I, and that is the letter taken out
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Céline Dion in a show's cast, from which somebody has pulled out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cast' is the anagram instruction and the company of a show at the same time, which is what holds the surface together. The 'one' dropped is the Roman numeral, not a performer.
annotation.definitionFit: Indolence is the settled habit of avoiding effort, which is laziness under a longer name.

entries.clue: Language from mum, say, when A&E switch over tablets at the outset (9)

indicatorNotes.switch: to switch two things is to have them change places, so the pair trade positions
indicatorNotes.at the outset: the outset is the very beginning, so these letters go to the front

blocks.note: ecstasy tablets are Es, one E each
a mum is one example of a PARENT; the A and the E change places
o = over in a cricket scorebook

annotation.surface: At the start of a shift, A&E hands the pills over.
annotation.walkthrough: A&E is the British hospital's accident and emergency department on the surface; in the wordplay it is only the letters A and E, told to trade places inside a word 'mum, say' has defined by example.
annotation.definitionFit: Esperanto is a language — the one invented in the 1880s to serve as everybody's second tongue.

entries.clue: Eco-friendly facts about drilling (5)

indicatorNotes.drilling: a drill bores into the middle of something, and that is where these letters go

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information — the facts
re = about, as at the head of a memo

annotation.surface: Environmentally sound information about drilling for oil.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' is the letters rather than the instruction, which is the neat swap here: the instruction is 'drilling'. Gen, for information, comes out of wartime services slang.
annotation.definitionFit: Green is the everyday word for anything eco-friendly — green energy, green policies.

entries.clue: Antique sabre – every now and then American cuts with it (7)

indicatorNotes.every now and then: now and then is not every time, so the letters are taken at intervals
indicatorNotes.cuts: to cut into something is to open it up and get inside

blocks.note: every second letter of s-A-b-R-e
someone chic is with it — stylish
a = American

annotation.surface: An old sword, and the American who now and then slices with it.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash lets 'sabre' look like part of the definition while it is working for the wordplay. 'With it' as slang for fashionable dates from the 1960s, which is half the joke.
annotation.definitionFit: Archaic and antique both describe something belonging to an age long gone, and both are adjectives.

entries.clue: See 1
Better speak with a married priest first (10)

indicatorNotes.first: what comes first stands at the head of the answer, ahead of everything else

blocks.note: used literally
m = married, as on a form
Eli is the priest who brought up Samuel in the Old Testament
to orate is to speak formally

annotation.surface: Advice to have a word with the married priest before anyone else.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Better' is the verb, to improve, not the comparative the surface is reaching for. Eli, priest at Shiloh, is one of the handful of Bible names every setter keeps to hand.
annotation.definitionFit: To ameliorate a situation is to better it; the definition is the same transitive verb as the answer.

entries.clue: Spooner’s drunk talk – it could confirm pregnancy (4,3)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer instead of replacing it: what is named is the structure whose appearance on an early scan settles the question.

indicatorNotes.Spooner’s: the Reverend Spooner's trademark slip was to exchange the opening sounds of two words, so that is what must be undone here

blocks.note: a drunk is a soak and to talk is to yak; swap the opening sounds of the pair

annotation.surface: The Reverend Spooner on the conversation of a drunkard.
annotation.walkthrough: Spooner clues want the pair of words first, so hunt for those: a soak, and to yak. William Spooner was an Oxford don whose tangled announcements made him famous.
annotation.definitionFit: On an early ultrasound the yolk sac is the first structure visible inside the gestational sac, so seeing it confirms a pregnancy is under way.

entries.clue: See 8
Liking a street in middle of Cheltenham (5)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' drops what comes before it inside what comes after
indicatorNotes.middle of: only the letters at the centre of the word are wanted, and the rest are discarded

blocks.note: used literally
st = street in an address
the two central letters of chelTEnham

annotation.surface: A fondness for one particular road in the centre of Cheltenham.
annotation.walkthrough: Cheltenham, a spa town in Gloucestershire, is here only for its middle — ten letters, so the centre comes out as a tidy pair rather than a single one.
annotation.definitionFit: A taste for something is a liking for it: 'she has a taste for opera' takes either noun.

entries.clue: Bird’s thigh bone discovered (3)

indicatorNotes.discovered: read as dis-covered, it means stripped of its covering, so the letters at either end come off

blocks.note: the femur is the thigh bone
the F and the R that cover it are taken away

annotation.surface: Somebody has dug up a bird's thigh bone.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue turns on splitting one word: dis-covered, with the cover taken off. Three-letter entries are usually where a setter hides that kind of trick.
annotation.definitionFit: The emu is a bird — the big flightless Australian one — so the definition names the family it belongs to.

entries.clue: Shout with gun going off – it’s not called for (8)

indicatorNotes.going off: a gun going off explodes, and an explosion scatters whatever it touches

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A shout and a gun going off, neither of them wanted.
annotation.walkthrough: Look at the fodder: 'shout' and 'gun' are a shotgun with one letter adrift, which is how the surface stays so natural while carrying an anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: Advice that is unsought was never asked for, which is exactly what 'not called for' says of it.

entries.clue: Trouble with Daily Telegraph’s leaders stopping supplement (3,2)

indicatorNotes.leaders: the leader of a word is the letter at its head, the one out in front
indicatorNotes.stopping: to stop a gap is to plug it, so these letters are pushed into the middle

blocks.note: ado is fuss or trouble — much ado about nothing
the initials of the British national newspaper

annotation.surface: The Daily Telegraph's bosses blocking a supplement, to everyone's annoyance.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves of the clue mean two things: 'leaders' is senior management on the surface and initial letters underneath, while 'supplement' is a magazine insert on the surface and a verb in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: To supplement a total is to add to it, and both are the transitive verb for topping something up.

entries.clue: Remains when Oscar leaves largest city in Michigan, America (8)

indicatorNotes.leaves: what leaves is gone, so that letter is no longer among the ones you write

blocks.note: Detroit is the biggest city in the state of Michigan
Oscar is O in the radio alphabet, and O is the letter that goes
US = America

annotation.surface: An Academy Award being carried out of Detroit.
annotation.walkthrough: Oscar is the radio alphabet's O, from the same list that supplies Charlie, Tango and Victor — a statuette only on the surface. Take it out of the city, then let America follow.
annotation.definitionFit: Detritus is the rubble and debris a process leaves behind, which is what remains names as a plural noun.

entries.clue: Cancel theatre’s Cinderella following cuts (7)

indicatorNotes.following cuts: cuts trim away the ends, and what is left standing after them is the run of letters you want

blocks.note: the letters run on from the middle of the first word into the second, straight across the apostrophe and the space

annotation.surface: A theatre dropping its pantomime after the funding is cut.
annotation.walkthrough: Cinderella is the staple British pantomime, which is why a theatre would have one to lose in the first place. Punctuation counts for nothing in a hidden run: theat-RE’S CIND-erella.
annotation.definitionFit: To rescind an order is to cancel it; both are the verb for revoking something already issued.

entries.clue: Enough to support son, 17 (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a cross-reference: 17 is the entry at 17 across, whose answer TASTE is the word being defined.

indicatorNotes.support: in a down entry whatever does the supporting has to sit underneath the thing it is holding up

blocks.note: s = son
ample means enough and a bit over

annotation.surface: Money enough to keep a son going.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma does the damage: 'son, 17' looks like a boy and his age, and is really son plus a pointer to another entry. Down clues stack, so the supporting piece goes below.
annotation.definitionFit: To sample a dish is to taste it, which is the word waiting at 17 across.

entries.clue: Perhaps Deborah Meaden’s doctor detailed extreme suffering (6)

indicatorNotes.detailed: split it as de-tailed and it means with the tail removed, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: dr = doctor
agony is extreme suffering, docked of its last letter

annotation.surface: Deborah Meaden's doctor spelling out some terrible illness.
annotation.walkthrough: Dragons' Den is the BBC show in which entrepreneurs pitch to a panel of millionaire investors, and Deborah Meaden has sat on it for years. 'Detailed' is de-tailed: one letter short at the back.
annotation.definitionFit: Deborah Meaden is one of the investors on BBC television's Dragons' Den, where the panel are known as the dragons — so she is an example of one.

entries.clue: Tense during drama initially directed like some soaps? (7)

indicatorNotes.during: whatever happens during something happens inside it, between its start and its end
indicatorNotes.initially: initially means at the very start, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: a scene is a unit of drama
t = tense in grammar
the opening letter of directed

annotation.surface: A tense passage of drama, directed the way soap operas are.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Soaps' are the bars in the bathroom, not the serials the rest of the surface is busy filming — drama, scene and direction are all there to keep you in the studio.
annotation.definitionFit: Scented soap is soap that has been perfumed, and the question mark concedes that only some of it is.

entries.clue: Powerless monkey – one seen in a circus? (5)

indicatorNotes.Powerless: powerless means without power, and power is what the letter p stands for

blocks.note: to monkey with something is to tamper with it
p = power, and it is the letter dropped

annotation.surface: A feeble monkey, of the sort you might see under the big top.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Monkey' is the verb, not the animal the circus invites you to picture: to monkey with something is to interfere with it. The definition has a different beast in mind altogether.
annotation.definitionFit: The tamer is the circus performer who works the lions, so 'one seen in a circus' names a person rather than an act.

entries.clue: See 1
Modern day translation of Latin essentially Your Worship (9)

indicatorNotes.translation of: a translation gives you the same thing in a different arrangement of words, and here the letters come out rearranged
indicatorNotes.essentially: the essence of a word is what sits at its heart, so only the middle letters are used

blocks.note: AD, anno domini, is how the modern era is dated
anagram fodder
the middle letters of yOUr
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A present-day rendering of some Latin, addressed to Your Worship.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Your Worship' is how a mayor or a magistrate is addressed in Britain, which is what puts the surface in a council chamber. Only the second word of it is the definition; the first gives up its middle.
annotation.definitionFit: Adulation is praise poured on somebody past all proportion — worship of a person rather than a god.

entries.clue: Distributing small – not large – handouts (4)

indicatorNotes.Distributing: to distribute is to hand things out one by one to different places, which is what happens to these letters
indicatorNotes.not: 'not large' says the letter standing for large is absent

blocks.note: SMALL less one L, leaving four letters to rearrange
l = large, and that is the letter dropped
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Handing out modest donations rather than lavish ones.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Distributing' shuffles the letters and describes charitable giving at once, so the clue never sounds like an anagram. The letter dropped is the one on a clothing label.
annotation.definitionFit: Alms are the money and food given to the poor, so they are handouts in the old charitable sense.

entries.clue: See 8
Kind to insect assuming one might be found under a pillow? (4,5)

annotation.definition: one might be found under a pillow?
annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer rather than standing in for it: what is named is the thing a child leaves there for the fairy to collect.

indicatorNotes.assuming: to assume something is to take it on, and here the word takes these letters on board inside itself

blocks.note: a moth is an insect
people of your ilk are people of your kind
used literally

annotation.surface: Sparing an insect you suspect is under your pillow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Kind' is the noun, ilk, not the adjective the surface is being — and the insect swallows it whole along with the little word after it. The definition is pointing at the fairy who leaves a coin.
annotation.definitionFit: A child's first set of teeth are the ones that fall out and get left under the pillow in exchange for a coin.

entries.clue: Keen – having second go after wasting first (5)

indicatorNotes.wasting: something wasted away has gone, so the letter named is lost from the word

blocks.note: a mo is a moment — half a mo
a go is a TURN, which loses the letter at its front

annotation.surface: Eager for another turn, having squandered the first one.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Keen' is the verb here — to keen is to wail aloud over the dead, an Irish word long since naturalised — not the adjective the surface wants. 'Mo' is the British half a mo.
annotation.definitionFit: To keen is to lament the dead out loud, so it names the act of grieving that the answer covers more broadly.
